top_comments.author: @matrodfpv
top_comments.text:
Just wanted to share:
The "film look" is actually more to do with the TRANSITION from darks to lights within the dynamic range (obviously the more latitude, the better).  "Highlight roll-off."  Film stock has a bee very smooth and gradual transition from dark to lights, especially in the highlight region.  This is the top factor that digital cameras fight to master, and why cameras like the Alexa and RED's are so sought after.

An important note, with the above in mind, is that trying to achieve the "film look" does not REQUIRE you to not let your highlights blow out.  I think this is worried about too much.  If we look closely at older films, like Scarface for example, there are scenes where the highs are most definitely blown out in some areas, but it works for the scene.  So I think that's an important and interesting point to remember. 

This is not a specific criticism or critique on any particular part of this video, I just really enjoy talking about these things and was prompted by the section talking about dynamic range.  Needless to say, this video's very informative and accurate.

I think there's been enough time to finally reveal the secret. We didn't shoot Niko with the arrow. The shot you see in the BTS was actually VFX. The arrow was already in the vest when he put it on. Had that been a real shot, the arrow would have penetrated at least 2 inches into his chest and we would have rushed to the hospital. It would be an incredibly stupid thing to do. 
This was just a prank on viewers for fun but we definitely do not recommend others trying it for real, it's not safe.

top_comments.text:
For those of you that noticed the extra noise, here's a bit of an explanation-

We shot this at 3k (A quarter of what the camera is capable of. Four 3k patches of area make a 6k patch of area), between the ISO of 2000 and 4000. Why the super high ISO?  Because we ended up being pretty underexposed with the cloud cover and the aperture and shutter settings used on camera.  Even so, the color accuracy and tonal range of the Dragon held up, even though the footage got a bit grainy.  We could have done noise removal, but the grain didn't really bother us, so we figured let it ride!

top_comments.author: @SirWrender
top_comments.text:
I'm catching up on all the comments now and realize that everyone is pointing out that it'd be easier to turn Obie into a 3D layer and call it a day. Well... you're absolute right. That's my bad for using the example I did. In this situation that WOULD be easier, but that's not the point of this quick tip. This tip is applicable to many other reasons than tracking. In fact I regrettably admit tracking an object into a shot is probably the least useful reason for using this tip. 

The point I was trying to make is that sometimes you need the 2D information from a 3D null, and the solution for that is NOT straightforward or obvious. You can't just link 2D layers to 3D nulls. I wish this feature was built in, but it's not. Sometimes you have an effect that you want to link to a 3D null so that it always sticks to where your null is, but the effect doesn't work in 3D because it's 2D only. This is for situations like that. Or sometimes you just want to point track a shot, you just need the position, but you don't want to babysit the shot as it tracks. This is quicker, trust me. 

TL;DR - Yes, making the layers 3D is easier for THIS example, that's my fault for not having a better exampl

To address the many questions about syncing on the 360 footage:

The stitching isn't really the problem, it's just the syncing of the different shots together. We've already figured out the best method, and it requires NO extra stuff. 
Ring lights, mirror bowls, mega clappers, fog horns (lol), all work but we either don't have what's needed or it's not worth the effort. 
My reasoning for the helmet was to get everything overexposed at the same time, which for the most part actually worked! It just had a couple weird issues preventing it from being perfect. Besides, our eventual solution is like a hundred times easier.

videos.title: New Hoverboard!

top_comments.author: @CorridorCrew
top_comments.text:
It's actually really simple why they're called "hoverboards". That's what happens when there are over a dozen different companies all basically producing the same core design (AlienBoard, IOHawk, Nanoboards, Swagway, etc) of a Chinese product with the dumb name "self-balancing two wheeled scooter". Combine that with their explosion in popularity in THE year when people are hungry for anything Back to the Future related.

So as these things become more and more popular, with each one belonging to a different company, people needed a universal name like "bicycle" or "car" and unfortunately they just started using the name "hoverboard". I know it's stupid. OBVIOUSLY they don't hover. But I mean, take headphones for example. They're not phones for your head, they're ear-speakers, right? I bet if you think about it you'll find a bunch of things that have names that don't LITERALLY represent what they do. 

I think most people are just salty that they don't have real hoverboards, with these wheeled versions being poor substitutes in their eyes. But ultimately, it's a little silly to get upset over what people call them.

top_comments.text:
I partially disagree about Rogue One.

While I agree about Jyn, I liked seeing the side of the rebels we hadn't seen. 
We always see this "Smiling cheering" rebels that do all the right things, but in the first moments of the movie we see some of the darker decisions the rebels have to make. 
There were things that hit and things that missed, but I really enjoyed the film...didn't attach with Jyn at all though. Figured everyone died since we've never heard of the characters before, and I was not disappointed with how it was done.

I don't look at Jyn as being a "main character."

You say she never made a hard choice, but I don't think she HAD to do any of what she did, but that ambition to see her father again is what pushed her through the movements. 
I guess I see this as an ensemble piece that is brought together because of one catalyst. Whether it be to writing, diversity, or the force.  

How many people do you know, that have Han Solo as their favorite instead of Luke or Leia?...Or Vader? I personally really connected with Cassian Andor, especially when he speaks about being born into this War.  We connect with who we connect with. different strokes for different folks, I gue

top_comments.author: @CorridorCrew
top_comments.text:
Hey Everyone! *Parts list for the drone is in the description!* _Explanation here_:

The drone I built is a modified Inductrix Blade, most commonly referred to as a "Tiny Whoop". You can buy fully built kits, DIY kits, or buy the individual parts and assemble it together like I did. You will also need a radio transmitter (the controller) and some FPV goggles to view the camera feed. You can also just use a little monitor screen that has a radio antenna attached. I already had these from when I started getting into racing drones last year. If you go the build-it-yourself route you will want to watch a lot of tutorials and will need a soldering iron. It wasn't as hard as I expected it to be though ;)

I was flying in what's called "*Acro*" mode, meaning that it does *_not_* fly like a DJI drone. If you set it to "level" mode, it will behave that way, but in acro mode it will not self-correct so you can easily do things like flips and barrel rolls, but also makes it way more difficult to fly. If you press forward on the sticks, it will continue to go forward until it's upside down haha. I've started learning how to do flips and stuff but I need to set better PIDs.

The main components

videos.title: What Memorial Day means to us

top_comments.author: @Rappasta
top_comments.text: im fron italy, my granpa served in ww2 and actually our city survived because of the american arrival ( in verona ), so thank you

top_comments.author: @TinyWorlds
top_comments.text:
I'm from Germany. My great-great-grandpa died in the war and was never really found, and my great-grandma kept searching for him their whole life. My grandma had to flee from approaching troops in a boxwagon without food and later over the frozen sea. All of that while she was still a child. And they were lucky, the order was to let civilians stay in the city, despite the frontline getting closer. All soldiers went away tho .. And my grandpa fished out corpses out of the river from the city of Dresden, once even a whole family bound together to drown.
War sucks. I don't want to memorize soldiers for their battles. Maybe as people, but it's not something I want to glorify.
Sure there are people that were "good" and defended people, but once it goes from defending to attacking I don't believe in the good of any army and the people directing it.
That said, I know most Americans have a bit different relation to war and soldiers than Germans, but if war was in your country for generations, you change your view on soldiers ..

This video is incorrect. We know about direct ads because we also have them, it's what informed us to make that video, because when we get the yellow mark our direct ads still DO NOT run. 

For clarity, our MCN sells ads directly on our content, just like ABC does on Kimmel, but YouTube is always the middle man. They are completely involved in the process and it uses their ad system. They make 45% on all sales and approve all sales, just like regular ads. The only difference here, which has already been confirmed to us by YouTube, is that Jimmy Kimmel (and a select few other channels, mostly owned by big media) have special exceptions that bypass their ad policy so they would never be demonetized. Since our video has been posted, they have confirmed to us that they are working to close that exception because their ad policy should be consistently enforced across the board.

Regarding their comments about censorship. What else would you call it? Rewarding some speech and punishing others? top_comments.author: @CorridorCrew
top_comments.text: The goal of this video was not to see if the iPhone X was as good as a RED. Obviously it won’t be. Instead, what we wanted to discover was how close (or far apart) they were in quality, and what kind of differences exist between the two. Smartphone cameras have improved tremendously over the years, but cinema cameras haven’t been standing still either. What we found is that compression is still an image quality killer for the iPhone, but color science and resolution have improved dramatically. As Sam said, the iPhone X is probably better than any camera we used before 2011, and the current Epic-W with the Helium sensor is surprisingly cutting edge and versatile.

top_comments.text: I am writing a paper on warranty void stickers and how they are in some ways illegal. There is an act called the Magnuson-Moss warranty act and it states that (for ex:) if you break your phones screen, you can replace it with any screen you choose and it will not invalidate the warranty. this prevents companies from "tie-in sales" which force you to buy apples phone screen compared to the affordable china competition in order to maintain a valid warranty. since you haven't physically damaged the product (except Wren and those clips) and the only thing you "broke" was the sticker, your warranty should still be in tact. I'm only a freshman in college and I am more likely wrong than not, but I wanted to give my two cents anyway. If Corridor reads this I would like to ask if Jake can do some research and do one of his lawyer rants and maybe put it in a video. I love your video's!

top_comments.author: @LadyCinnamonGirl
top_comments.text: I worked on "Pleasantville". The burning tree scene are all shot in b&w.  We had a poly over the fence and, with proprietary software, then pulled out yellow on one  luminance level. In the long shots the yellow on the house was done the same. The tree was done the same way with and more complicated poly over the fire a a little smoke and several different luminance levels pulled in different intensities of that same yellow and one one level slight red which you see better in the scene where Tony walks out the door. In that shot there is a poly on his shirt that has the yellow pulled out more subtly.  You would be surprised how many plots are in these shots with little things of yellow are pulled. The effect is supposed to be the fire is the only thing in color, but the color does reflect off of the b&w world.  They didn't want a lot of oranges or reds just that hint of red and different intensities of yellow

I'm one of the VFX artist credited for the " interior rolling ball scene" in THE ROBOT.

Air quality engineer here (yup, we exist):

1: This instrument is probably crap. Using this kind of instrument is like saying "it's between 0 and 50". A real instrument (used by France or the US EPA) is roughly the size of a small fridge and costs between 20-40k $. A state of the art one costs 400k $. They also take dayyys to calibrate and get working, need stable conditions, etc...

2: Yes, there's no way the PM2.5 was at 5 µg/m3 near that highway

3: BUT the most important thing, you guys measured the "instant" concentration. You pulled the instrument out and measured. But PM10 or PM2.5 are measured on year or day average. Let's say your instrument is decent, you'd have to let it run for at least a day (outside or in the office) without moving it and in stable conditions and see what the daily average is. The World Health Organization recommends that PM2.5 doesn't exceed 10 µg/m3... on a year average (25 µg/m3 daily average).

4: Nico, you're right, LA's air right now is probably way better than it was a few decades ago. You're also right about the instrument being a particle reader and ignoring all the rest.

top_comments.text:
Recent interviews have revealed;
- The redesign was headed by a fan artist, turned official animation director, Tyson Hesse. A well known name in the Sonic fan community for his fanart, time spent working on the official Sonic Comic series, and his work creating and directing 2D animations for the official Sonic social media team (See Sonic Mania's opening cutscene which was created almost entirely by himself, as well as his work as a director for 'Sonic Mania Adventures', and 'Team Sonic Racing Overdrive')
- Most of the animation was redone, however some things were able to be salvaged and worked onto the new model.
- The original movie design was indeed pressured by the studio, who knew fans wouldn't like it. However they assumed that people would come to accept it. No surprise.
- The delay came after a meeting was held with Sega.
- They started the redesign from the head, and worked down.
- It took them 5 months to get to this point, with little to no real crunch time.

Serious quesiton: Could the reason these features aren't available be related to the generation/age of the consumers using them?  The people who can afford $20k cameras might not have a lot of overlap with people who grew up with smart phones and are used to features we find in our smart phones.


I went to school for animation, and most of my instructors came from the generation of Tex Avery and Looney Tunes.  They would actively discourage students from doing anything 'anime style'.  My roommate ignored them, and strictly did things in an anime style, and was continuously criticized for it.  She ended up getting hired before even graduating, and today a majority of modern animation has influences that come from anime.   I can envision a similar thing happening in the camera industry-  as people like yourselves start replacing the older generation of filmmakers, the industry will have to adapt and provide the products you want.

top_comments.author: @Hevesh5
top_comments.text: This is seriously so impressive! As a domino artist (thanks for showing some of my projects in the beginning!), I’m amazed at how realistic it looks. Usually these physics domino simulations look clearly animated, but the extra level of details you put into the lighting, surface imperfections, size, and sound were really well done. The only thing that seemed off was the domino drop at 11:22 from the door to the circle field on the ground - that was just too clean of a fall xD Usually dominoes would bounce and make dominoes fly everywhere on impact, especially from that high up on the ground. But really, this was awesome and I very much enjoyed hearing the thought process behind it! If you need a pro Domino Artist to help out with some designs, just let me know! Can’t wait to see what you make in the next one!

After a few minutes, the (white) proprietor behind the counter asked us to leave because we were making his boss "nervous" and he likewise did not want to make any customers nervous. We had to wait outside in the 90-degree weather. I probably needn't mention that I'm white and my friend is black.  Anyway, I got pissed and started to argue with the guy, but my friend just shook his head and said "It's OK. Let's just go outside..."  That started the discussion. I cannot know what it's like to be in his position, but I think I got just the slightest hint that day. top_comments.author: @Aer0Alex
top_comments.text:
I fly F-18s and can provide some insight to the last 3 videos. These videos are footage from the FLIR. At the top left you can see the FOV "NAR" which is the smallest FOV available for the sensor. So it's zoomed in as far as it can go without a digital zoom. The number beneath "IR" in the top center is the degrees in azimuth the FLIR is looking in relation to the aircraft, and the number on the left is degrees in elevation. On the right you can see 'X.X RNG' which is the range in nautical miles to the tracked object, and below that is the closure to the object in knots (ie the aircraft is closing in on that object at that airspeed). On the bottom right is the altitude of the aircraft, and the bottom left is the Mach number of the aircraft 'M 0.XX'

So for the first video, putting all those numbers together, you guys made a valid assessment that the object isn't moving that much. What's interesting to me, is that unless they were already looking in the area and saw the 'bird,' there would've been no way for them to see it in the first place. The symbology on the right tells me that the FLIR is in a mode set to track air targets, meaning that the FLIR had to be cued to that object vi

top_comments.author: @SirWrender
top_comments.text:
Thank you so much everyone for watching! There are a thousand more things I would’ve loved to say and include in this video. There are so many clarifications and footnotes to include. I had an entire moment talking about the benefits of nuclear but as with everything else, it detracted too much from the point I was trying to make.  

A large part of my struggle making this was figuring out what the point of this was. How can I simplify such a complicated scope of a topic into something that is easy to understand, correct, informative, and entertaining enough for people to stick around? It was hard. I hope I’ve done that. 

Of course there are huge problems surrounding materials, toxicity, and emissions when it comes to the production of solar tech and lithium ion batteries. But these are just that… problems. We can solve them!! We WILL solve them!! I’m trying to inspire the right people who will help us discover new solutions.

I don’t anticipate changing anyone’s mind if they don’t believe in climate change. I’m hoping well reasoned folks who ARE interested in a better future see this and realize the simple fundamental realities of what’s POSSIBLE before getting lost in the weeds

top_comments.author: @CraigGood
top_comments.text:
This is nice, but a few historical details aren't quite right. I was part of the crew that made this - and I'm in that group photo you showed.

John did not go to England to measure the set and record where the lights were. Someone else got that info for us. Motion blur was invented in the Computer Division, and we were never part of ILM.

We rendered the highlights as a separate element so that ILM Optical could tweak them, and if you look carefully all of the floating bits of glass are slightly convex, which allowed a more pleasing reflection of the environment. (When Barry Levinson asked in dailies for it to look "more religious" we all panicked, but Dennis Muren just had Optical add 2 more clicks of diffusion to the glow pass.)

A detail you might like is that the candles and stands in the foreground of that tracking shot are all CGI.

That rack focus shot was so expensive to compute that I spent 2 weeks at CCI headquarters in Orange County rendering just the last 2/3 of that shot on borrowed computers overnight. Meanwhile, Bill Reeves (the bearded guy in the photo with John) rendered the first third. I had to fly down with two giant disk packs which each could hold about 300 M

videos.title: Watch this before you give up on your dreams...

top_comments.author: @vfxwithjordan
top_comments.text:
Hey guys, thanks for watching!

Just wanted to add my thoughts for those out there who maybe don't even know what it is they WANT to learn in the first place.

When it comes to picking a direction it can feel daunting, and the possibilities endless, but I believe a great first step is trying to figure out where you want to be in one year, five years, and ten years from now. What brings you joy? What do you see others doing and think, “I want to do THAT”.

In the 3D world, for example, there’s so many different paths you can take from modeling, texturing, lighting, compositing, or even just being a generalist who does a little bit of everything. Each of these paths lead to different end goals and the same is true in almost any field. So before starting down one specific path think about what makes you tick, and most importantly what makes you happy.

As I mentioned in the video, my initial plan was to go to USC and become an editor at Warner Brothers. I had no other dreams of doing anything else, and getting rejected completely ruined my plans. But by leaning on the skills I’d learned in working towards that initial goal, I changed course and used those skills to spur me on

videos.title: What Makes Anime Great and why Hollywood Ruins it

top_comments.author: @OverlySarcasticProductions
top_comments.text: It almost feels like a lot of these adaptations don't know HOW to capture that Certain Something from the source material, and they're aware of that, so they purposefully compensate in ways that accidentally highlight their own issues. Cowboy Bebop does some interesting things with lighting and shadow and they TRY with the choreography, which even looks and feels solid in places - but it feels like they can't replicate the extremely dynamic *camera* and how it moves around in the fights and action scenes, so instead they just dutch angle it every couple of shots. Ghost in the Shell makes the colors dimmer and darker, and everything in the gunfire scene so dark you can't even see what's happening - which feels like cinematographic insecurity, like they HAVE to keep it dark because they don't think it looks good. The strength of animation is you can literally just draw anything and put the camera anywhere, and these adaptations feel like they're actively frustrated that they don't know how to do the same thing. -R

top_comments.text:
Hi! Italy here! My Granpa's brother worked as a runner and assistaint on The Palm Beach Story. I had the chance to hear the full story about this shot, and it is absolutely mind-blowing.
He was there during the 3 weeks needed to make this.

During the production, they initially attempted to manually create camera motion using some ingenious gear mechanism to maintain a constant speed. Countless takes were done in a single day, and they thought they had nailed it. However, when they got to the lab (no monitors back then), they discovered three major problems:

First, the camera angle was off. People in the background were caught in the transition line between takes, and no single shot matched perfectly.

Second, they realized that for a seamless result, they had to start the shot with the camera in motion and end it the same way, which meant no cool ending titles.

Finally, the transition line between the takes was quite visible, as they had no idea how to blend it seamlessly.

As a result, they dedicated an entire week in the lab, tirelessly inventing a method to blend the transition line between two shots. They were thrilled, thinking they had come up with a film editing

top_comments.author: @aSinisterKiid
top_comments.text: I think I have noticed something that is partially responsible for the uncanny valley feeling in the faces. The lack of forehead movement. Because of the rig you guys wear to capture the facial movements, that strap and headgear basically cut off your forehead movement. And humans have a lot of movement in their forehead with the skin and the muscles that move and wrinkle along with the rest of your face. Those little nuances of forehead wrinkles or furrowing of the brow are missing because its just a flat forehead due to the rig. That could be a huge improvement on the overall feeling if you could find a way to get the forehead movement back.

top_comments.author: @TomMartinek
top_comments.text: I did the shot in AI around the 10:55 mark.  When we removed the blue screen material on his head, we had to fill in the missing background from a clean plate.  I decided that no matter how well we lined up the plate, it was going to be impossible to not see the split around the head - so I just split in the whole right side of frame from the clean plate and put the split off the center of the frame.   (The girl running up to the camera at around 11:20 was also the first time I ever saw a match move get a standing ovation in dailies.).  I was also in charge of the CG Teddy and the renders for him took over 24 hours a frame.  When I was told I had to come up with a faster way to render him, I setup an all texture version of him that rendered in 3 minutes.  I did a test for VFX supes Dennis Muren and Scorr Farrar that had side by side renders of the real fur and the fake one and they couldn't tell them apart.  From that moment on, we never rendered the full fur Teddy ever again.

top_comments.text:
The Temple of Doom bridge shot has so much more to it, and it got covered by one of the best VFX documentaries 'How To Film The Impossible'. When the crew are casually saying that the falling bodies are being rotoscoped, you have to remember this was done on film, that meant blowing up the frames, drawing lines around the objects onto transparent acetate, and then painting over the outlines to make the mask, rephotographing these onto 35mm film and then finally compositing the whole lot on an optical printer. 
When hanging off the cliff there's a lot of optical elements that needed to be combined, and stuntmen falling off watch matched by puppeteers so they could transition from the real people to the models as they fell from one side of the frame to the other.
It's a fantastic documentary because it shows just how much work was needed before digital compositing became commonplace.

videos.title: This Invention Made Disney MILLIONS, but Then They LOST It!

top_comments.author: @RustyGellerSteadicam
top_comments.text: I was one of the last people at Disney to use the Sodium Vapor light system. It was on "Something Wicked This Way Comes" in 1982 or 3. I was an vfx AC at the studio. The prisim was held under license from Rank.  It was a hallowed object. It was kept in a steel box and it was studio policy that 2 AC's had to be with it at all times when it was removed from the storage locker. We both carried it to the stage, then carefully inserted it into the 2-strip camera. It was never left alone on stage, we took turns leaving for lunch, the john, etc.  It hadn't been used for years but we had a series of tough matte jobs to shoot so they dusted off the old gear. I was aware I was watching a bit of history.  The key was the didymium filter in the prism. That thing has to be around somewhere. Technically, Rank would still own it.

top_comments.author: @MonsieurDoge

top_comments.author: @Nighthawkinlight
top_comments.text: FYI, your sodium lamps should be upsidedown or sideways for longevity. If you have the electrodes on the bottom they'll get dripped on by sodium which will eventually cause the bulb to fail. If used properly LPS bulbs will last pretty much forever. This is a very clever technique. Well done

Hi, I'm a muppet performer (I play Dr. Teeth’s dad Gerald Teeth Sr.) and NY Henson shop builder. Marionette puppeteers performed Kermit’s and Piggy’s bikes. The bikes and puppets were rigged to a controller connected to a crane. The wide of all the bikes was done by connecting all the bikes. You can see the connections if you look closely enough. We still do a lot of practical puppetry FX in our films and TV shows. However, since everyone expects there to be CG, it gets looked over as a digital effect.

A great example is the show Donkey Hodie. In it, a puppet juggles. There is no VFX. All practical and in camera. I started my professional career as a VFX artist, so I can say that in TV/Film puppetry, the same saying exists. If you didn't see the effect, then we have done our job right.

Da Vinci was obsessed in the last years of his life with trying to draw water in movement - eddies, cascades, currents. top_comments.author: @mixphantom0101
top_comments.text: Finally!  A VFX shot I worked on!  Jason X frozen face was meant to be a full on morph but I was "slap comping" the VFX shots on Quantel Henry for editorial so I just cut out the prop face, tracked it to the talent's face and did a simple cross dissolve!  The bubbles coming out of the nose sold the effect and the director approved it to be final comped in the Discreet Inferno.  The bubbles coming out of the nose were in the prop footage - so no rotoscoping of bubbles or particles involved.  Jason X is actually a part of film history as it was the first full length feature to be 100% digital pipeline - so every frame of film shot was scanned to 10 bit digital tape in 1080p HD so the edit, colour grade and VFX could all be working simultaneously!

videos.title: VFX Artist Reveals the TERRIFYING Speed of WILDFIRES

top_comments.author: @Random_White_Circle
top_comments.text:
FIREFIGHTER HERE:
that clip of the 737 "missing" wasn't a miss. When the fire line is an advancing erratic shape, then you drop ahead of it, not on the fire.

You drop the fire retardant on the fuel that you don't want to burn next.

Dropping on the fire would cut the fire down the middle like a knife, but the part beside new fuel will just advance and spread.


This is why you don't drop on the fire every time.

top_comments.author: @RuffinItAB
top_comments.text: As a Canadian wildland firefighter, the fires we are experiencing in fire prone landscapes are a completely new paradigm. People living in these areas need to understand the reality of the emerging extreme wildfire threat and work like this is immense in helping inform people. Thanks for your work in spreading information that could save lives, and to the people living in fire prone areas, don't be scared, be prepared.

top_comments.author: @BreakingW1ld
top_comments.text: 20 years of wildfire experience here in Australia. One thing you didn’t cover was ground slope. Your simulations had the fire spreading equally in all directions on the hill. It doesn’t work like that. Downhill fire travels slower as the fuel below it doesn’t get preheated as quickly. Fire running uphill, doubles its speed for every 10 degrees of slope. This is due to the preheating of fuels being closer to the flames, off gassing etc. watch fire creep downhill, then compare it to the fire running up a mountain.

videos.title: VFX Artists Debunk... REAL UFO Videos

top_comments.author: @CraigGood
top_comments.text: I animated cameras at Pixar for around 20 years. My rule of thumb (working at 24 fps) was that the fastest believable rehearsed reaction time for the camera operator was 4 frames. Any faster and it felt fake. On WALL-E I went a few frames longer when the operator was "surprised" by the action. It's amazing what a narrow range there is to play with there.

top_comments.author: @Gretchen_Trouble
top_comments.text: I saw a triangle glint about 15 years ago. I never thought it was aliens or anything, but it was always a bit unsettling having no idea what I saw. I screamed when I saw the clip you guys showed because I immediately knew that was what I saw years ago. Thanks for helping me put this decade long mystery to bed.

top_comments.author: @toweri_li
top_comments.text:
I was school-aged (at mid-70's, some 12-13 years, perhaps), living in Tampere, Finland. One night I saw an extremely bright yellowish star from my bedroom window, rising slowly at East by North-easterly direction, straight up, approximately 30-40 deg altitude. It steadily slowed down, coming to a full stop - which caught my attention. It was too bright to be an aeroplane and it had no navigation lights. As I was staring it, suddendly multiple smaller stars separated from it, forming a perfect circle, very slowly moving away from the main object.
I was flabbergasted. Astronomy was already one of my interests, so I knew it cannot be an astronomical phenomenon. I refused to believe it's a UFO. All lights slowly got fainter and finally disappeared in a few minutes.

It took me about 50 years to come to think about it seriously - and finally connect the dots:
Viewed from Tampere, central/south Finland, at East by North-east - Exact direction of Plesetsk cosmodrome!

That must have been a launch of a Soviet rocket with multiple boosters detaching.

videos.title: VFX Artists React to Bad & Great CGi 190

top_comments.author: @rixx46
top_comments.text:
You finally got to a movie I worked on.  

I was on the Canadian crew for SUPERMAN in 1977. We shot all the Young Superman scenes as well as the missile convoy at the end and the start of the Lois Lane earthquake stuff. Jeff East did his best running on those wires - they were driving 40MPH!  "You will believe a man can fly..." but run...?

Yes, we shot the wooden football out of an air canon -- we did it twice. The first time, the football nearly reached the grain elevators in the BG!  The second take worked better. 

As a set PA, I had to recover the wooden football. I kept it for over 35 years until I sold it a few years ago, along with some other bits and pieces at a prop auction for over $10,000!

5:38 BetterHelp isn’t real therapy; it’s a gig platform dressed up like one. Therapists are paid per message, not per meaningful session, which pushes them to handle too many clients and stay shallow just to keep up. Without proper oversight, there is no safeguard to catch mistakes, bad habits, or ethical breaches before they harm people.

Supervision is how real therapy protects patients. It means another qualified clinician regularly reviews the therapist’s work, offers guidance, and prevents harm. When a company skips that safety net, it turns mental health care into customer service that is fast, cheap, and dangerously unaccountable.

Edit: It's hilarious how true this statement has been proven true. Ppl saying it's not ai without even knowing what corridor crew is useing. This is wan move in comfyui. U just dont know what professional ai tools look like.

top_comments.author: @WalkerCloud
top_comments.text:
Since there are some recurring discussions in the comments weather or not this technique used "AI" or more specifically "Generative AI" here are some additional context:

This would not be possible if they did't use Generative AI.

They use what's called a "control net" to guide the motion as well as feeding the AI the reference image of the toy. But it is a generative AI model that generates the frames based on the guided motion and input image.

You can see the the faded in image of a program called "Comfy UI" during the montage, that program is used to give extra control inputs to Generative AI models, and those models themselves still need to be trained on massive data sets to function like any other gen AI model.

You can even see that the specific AI model they use here is called Wan Animate.

This model, like any Gen AI model, is also capable of generating matrial from only text prompts. But all gen AI models can also be guided in other ways, through various methods, to control the output they produce. Which is what's is done here.

I was the Virtual Art Department Supervisor on A Minecraft Movie, our team built the world of the film in Unreal during pre-production to assist the Art Department in visualising the set builds, as well as the extensions and surrounding environments. As seen in this video, it was also used for on-set comping with Nudge-Cam, and became the bed for the VFX on the film before being replaced with the beautifully rendered version you see in the end product of the film.

Saw a few comments about the map of the movie so I thought I'd chime in :)

We worked tightly with our Production Designer (the legendary Grant Major) to build out the full map of the film's locations so that each location the heroes travel to had full spatial continuity. When we started, I knew there would be fans who were committed to building a replica of the film's world, so it was really important you could see and feel how far we had travelled using natural landmarks as you do in the game. While I'm sure some of that detail was lost in post production (like recognising the exact same mountain across two shots) larger biome groups and regions in the distance should still match up.

top_comments.author: @AdamPFarnsworth
top_comments.text:
I wonder if Gaussian splats will age like early CGI. In 10–20 years, will people look back and say, “I didn’t notice as a kid, but this looks really splatty”?

*Edit* I see a lot of replies saying "It already looks splatty." Here's a response I typed out to someone and want to share it here, just to streamline responses lol:

That's kind of the point though (already looking splatty). In early CGI, we kind of accepted that pixelation "just happens" because of our limited technology. In the same way, perhaps splats will start being used heavily, and to an extent the general public will just think they're awesome because of the new techniques we can use, and simply accept the lower quality.

Granted, anyone watching this channel is going to be more dialed into details, but the general public might not even notice them, until they improve.

We're also spoiled a bit these days, having channels like this to break down and explain visual effects. I bet a lot more of us might have been more critical of the original Toy Story and VeggieTales if we have experts breaking down effects for us back then lol

top_comments.author: @Ericpot1969
top_comments.text: Hi Guys. Re THE PITT.  We shot the bridge sequence on September 17th.  The opening establishing beauty shots of Pittsburgh were actually taken from ND footage that was shot during season 1, the year before. For Season 2, That Morning, It was a 6 AM crew call and sunrise was 7:02 AM so we bracketed the drone work of the ambulance on the bridge first,  starting from near darkness as the sun Rose until it got too obviously past daybreak. And then started doing the tow work with the motorcycle on the bridge.  What you're seeing is a sequence that was actually shot in script order as the daylight progresses from 6 AM up until about 1:30 PM when we broke for lunch. The final shot of him walking into the hospital indeed was at 1 PM with hot light and front light. This is literally why we angled all of that coverage into the building and Foliage, knowing that we would have a better shot from a visual effect standpoint of fixing it rather than the original idea that would've looked straight down the street. top_comments.author: @rixx46
top_comments.text:
FINALLY, I have something to contribute!  I worked on DAYS OF HEAVEN as a PA when I was 20.  We dropped a mix of peanut shells and Sycamore seeds because their wing-like shape kept them spinning. 

THE FIRE SCENE: We were meant to shoot the fire over a few nights, with firebreak trenches dug into the field. The UK-based FX guy sprayed the wheat with diesel because he had no idea how easily it would burn.  As a result, THE ENTIRE FIELD CAUGHT FIRE and we had to scramble to film everything that night before it burned out in the midst of an uncontrolled inferno.  I was in the middle of it, swinging a wet sack with the other extras that night, surrounded by walls of flames. The house nearly burned down! It was madness!  Lucky no one was hurt.

The shot of the "dog" is a wild coyote that was in the field. The camera caught the shot by accident.  We would NEVER have intentionally risked an animal like that - no legit film would.  

It should be added that the great Nestor Almendros won the Oscar for his stunning cinematography.

top_comments.author: @hollywoodstoryboards7196
top_comments.text: I was the lead storyboard artist on I, Robot, from June 2002 to July 2003. That included 2 trips to Australia, where it was set to film with Nick Cage as Spooner. Filming shifted to Vancouver the day before Thanksgiving when Will Smith signed on (Fox wanted a star who could "Open" the picture). Not to spoil the contributions of the VFX people, but many of the "gags" in the film were imagined by the storyboard artists. The Robot getting crushed under the wheel was the idea of a young Irish artist named Warren Flannigan (Director Alex Proyas laughed when he saw Warren's drawing and said, "You're really sick!"). I was responsible for the idea of using the spherical wheels to spin the car to use centrifugal force to fling the robots off the car, as well as the ball wheel flying off the truck and into the tunnel. Myself and others contributed many more ideas and shots, including the overhead shot of Sonny illustrating his dream by using both hands at once, since he would not be limited by left or right-handedness. Storyboard artists get short shrift for many ideas in films that we pitch as part of our jobs. One time a director actually took credit for one of my ideas on the commentary t

top_comments.text: You guys might not realize it, but a lot of us in these comments look at Corridor the way you look at ILM. You may not have changed the film industry the way they did, but you've changed how we see this craft. You've inspired and taught every one of us. Thank you for being that for us.

top_comments.author: @astro_stellar
top_comments.text:
I feel like the reason why you are so universally loved by everyone in the industry, including the really big names, is because you are shining a light on the unsung artists, and their craft, love and passion they put into making us, the audience, dream when we go to the movies.

You have no reason of feeling out of your place, everything you have achieved is fully deserved, and I'm looking forward to see the legendary interviews!
